Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Physical Education Study Design, Units 3 and 4. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs, not VCAA syllabus numbering.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Use class resources and past examinations for official practice.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Classification of movement skills
points.detail: Classifying skills as fine or gross, discrete, serial or continuous, and open or closed, and justifying the classification with reference to the movement.

questions.q: Classify a netball shot for goal using three classification continua and justify each.
answer: Gross motor skill, because it uses large muscle groups of the legs, trunk and arms rather than small precise muscles alone.
Discrete, because it has a clear beginning and end.
Closed, because it is performed in a predictable environment with the shooter self-paced and no direct interference at the moment of release.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Stages of learning
points.detail: The cognitive, associative and autonomous stages, and the characteristics of performance, error rate, attention and feedback needs in each.

questions.q: Identify the stage of learning of an athlete who performs consistently, makes few errors and can scan the field while executing the skill, and describe the feedback they need.
answer: The athlete is in the autonomous stage of learning.
Performance is consistent and largely automatic, so attention is freed for tactical decisions and scanning the environment.
They require minimal, highly specific feedback, often intrinsic and focused on fine-tuning technique.
Coach feedback at this stage is best directed at strategy and at small technical refinements rather than basic execution.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Practice strategies
points.detail: Massed and distributed practice, blocked and random practice, and whole and part practice, and the situations in which each is appropriate.

questions.q: Compare blocked and random practice and state which suits a cognitive learner.
answer: Blocked practice repeats one skill many times consecutively, allowing the learner to groove the movement pattern.
Random practice varies the skill or the order of skills between attempts, which better replicates game conditions.
Blocked practice suits a cognitive learner, since repetition builds the basic motor pattern and reduces error rate.
Random practice produces better long-term retention and transfer, so it suits associative and autonomous learners.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Feedback
points.detail: Intrinsic and augmented feedback, knowledge of results and knowledge of performance, and the frequency and type appropriate to each stage of learning.

questions.q: Distinguish between knowledge of results and knowledge of performance, and explain which is more useful for a cognitive learner.
answer: Knowledge of results is information about the outcome of the movement, such as whether the shot went in.
Knowledge of performance is information about the quality of the movement itself, such as the position of the elbow at release.
A cognitive learner benefits most from knowledge of performance, because they cannot yet detect their own technical errors.
It should be delivered frequently, in simple terms and focused on one cue at a time to avoid overload.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Qualitative movement analysis
points.detail: The stages of preparation, observation, evaluation and error correction, and the use of video and observation to analyse technique.

questions.q: Outline the four stages of a qualitative movement analysis.
answer: Preparation: gather knowledge of the correct technique and the performer, and decide what to observe and from which angle.
Observation: view the movement several times from appropriate vantage points, often using video and slow motion.
Evaluation: compare the observed technique with the correct model to identify strengths and the most significant error.
Error correction: provide feedback and a corrective strategy, prioritising the error that will most improve performance.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Newton's laws applied to movement
points.detail: Inertia, acceleration and action-reaction applied to sporting movements, and the link between force, mass and acceleration.

questions.q: Apply Newton's third law and Newton's second law to a sprinter driving out of the blocks.
answer: Newton's third law: the sprinter applies a force backwards and downwards into the blocks, and the blocks apply an equal and opposite force forwards and upwards on the sprinter.
This ground reaction force propels the sprinter forwards.
Newton's second law: acceleration is proportional to the net force applied and inversely proportional to mass.
A greater force applied against the blocks therefore produces greater acceleration for a sprinter of a given mass.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Levers
points.detail: First, second and third class levers, the arrangement of fulcrum, force and resistance, and the trade-off between force and speed.

questions.q: Identify the lever class used in most human limb movements and explain the mechanical trade-off it produces.
answer: Most human limb movements use third class levers, in which the force is applied between the fulcrum and the resistance.
The force arm is shorter than the resistance arm, so the muscle must generate a force greater than the resistance being moved.
The trade-off is mechanical disadvantage in force but an advantage in speed and range of movement.
A small muscle contraction therefore produces a large, fast movement at the end of the limb, which suits throwing and kicking.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Force summation
points.detail: The sequencing and timing of body segments from largest to smallest, the use of the stretch-shorten cycle, and the transfer of momentum.

questions.q: Explain the principle of force summation and how a cricketer applies it when throwing.
answer: Force summation is the coordinated use of body segments to produce maximum force, sequenced from the largest and slowest to the smallest and fastest.
The movement begins with the legs and hips, transfers through the trunk, then the shoulder, elbow and finally the wrist and fingers.
Each segment must be timed so it begins at the point of peak velocity of the preceding segment, so momentum accumulates rather than being lost.
A stable base and a preparatory backswing also increase the range of motion over which force can be applied.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Angular momentum and rotation
points.detail: The relationship between moment of inertia and angular velocity, and the manipulation of body position to control rotation.

questions.q: Explain why a diver tucks during a somersault and extends before entry.
answer: Tucking brings the mass closer to the axis of rotation, reducing the moment of inertia.
Because angular momentum is conserved once airborne, a reduced moment of inertia produces an increased angular velocity, so the diver spins faster.
Extending before entry increases the moment of inertia again, slowing the rotation so the diver can control the position of entry.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Balance, stability and centre of gravity
points.detail: The effect of base of support, height of the centre of gravity, mass and the line of gravity on stability, and the trade-off with mobility.

questions.q: Explain how a wrestler maximises stability and why a sprinter in blocks adopts a less stable position.
answer: A wrestler widens the base of support and lowers the centre of gravity, keeping the line of gravity centred within the base.
Greater mass and a low, wide position make it harder for an opponent to move the line of gravity outside the base, so stability is high.
A sprinter deliberately raises the centre of gravity and shifts the line of gravity towards the front of the base.
This reduces stability but allows rapid acceleration in the intended direction, because the body is already falling forwards.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Projectile motion
points.detail: The effects of angle of release, speed of release and height of release on the flight path of a projectile.

questions.q: Name the three factors that determine the flight path of a projectile and state which has the greatest effect on distance.
answer: Angle of release, speed of release and height of release determine the flight path.
Speed of release has the greatest effect on the distance travelled, because horizontal displacement increases with the square of velocity.
Height of release above the landing point means the optimal angle is slightly less than 45 degrees.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — Movement skills and biomechanics
points.title: Coaching approaches and constraints
points.detail: Direct instruction and constraints-based approaches, and manipulating task, environmental and individual constraints to shape skill development.

questions.q: Explain a constraints-based coaching approach and give one example of manipulating a task constraint.
answer: A constraints-based approach designs practice conditions so that the desired movement or decision emerges, rather than instructing the athlete directly.
Constraints may be individual, such as the athlete's height or confidence, environmental, such as playing surface or weather, or task related.
Manipulating a task constraint could mean reducing the size of the playing area to increase the frequency of decisions under pressure.
The approach develops decision making and adaptability because the athlete solves the movement problem themselves.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: ATP as the energy currency
points.detail: The breakdown of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate to release energy for muscular contraction, and the need for continuous resynthesis.

questions.q: Explain why ATP must be continually resynthesised during exercise.
answer: ATP is the only immediately usable form of chemical energy for muscular contraction.
Stores of ATP within the muscle are very small and would be exhausted within one to two seconds of maximal effort.
The three energy systems therefore resynthesise ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate at rates matched to the intensity and duration of the activity.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: The ATP-PC system
points.detail: Fuel, rate and yield of ATP production, duration of maximal contribution, by-products and recovery of phosphocreatine stores.

questions.q: Describe the ATP-PC system in terms of fuel, rate, yield, duration and by-products.
answer: Fuel: phosphocreatine stored within the muscle.
Rate: the fastest of the three systems, producing ATP almost instantly, but the yield is very low at one ATP per molecule of phosphocreatine.
Duration: it is the predominant system for maximal efforts of roughly one to ten seconds.
By-products: heat and inorganic phosphate only, with no fatiguing metabolic by-product, and stores are largely replenished within two to three minutes of passive recovery.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: The anaerobic glycolysis system
points.detail: Fuel, rate, yield, duration of predominance, and the accumulation of hydrogen ions associated with metabolic acidosis.

questions.q: Describe the anaerobic glycolysis system and explain the fatigue it causes.
answer: Fuel: muscle glycogen and blood glucose, broken down without oxygen.
Rate: fast, though slower than the ATP-PC system, with a yield of about two ATP per molecule of glucose.
Duration: it is the predominant system for high intensity efforts of roughly ten seconds to one or two minutes.
The accumulation of hydrogen ions lowers muscle pH, causing metabolic acidosis, which interferes with enzyme activity and calcium binding and reduces force production.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: The aerobic system
points.detail: Fuels of carbohydrate, fat and protein, the rate and very high yield, the requirement for oxygen and the duration of predominance.

questions.q: Describe the aerobic system and explain why fat is used more heavily at lower intensities.
answer: Fuel: carbohydrate at higher intensities and fat at lower intensities, with protein contributing only in prolonged exercise.
Rate: the slowest of the three systems, but the yield is by far the highest, at roughly 36 to 38 ATP per molecule of glucose.
It is the predominant system beyond about two minutes and for all submaximal continuous exercise.
Fat requires more oxygen per unit of ATP produced than carbohydrate, so it can only predominate when intensity is low enough for oxygen supply to meet demand.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: Interplay of energy systems
points.detail: The simultaneous contribution of all three systems, with the predominant system determined by intensity and duration, and the shifts that occur within an activity.

questions.q: Describe the interplay of energy systems during a 400 metre sprint.
answer: All three systems contribute throughout; the question is which predominates at each point.
The ATP-PC system predominates for the first few seconds out of the blocks, providing the immediate rapid ATP for maximal acceleration.
Anaerobic glycolysis then predominates for the majority of the race, supporting high intensity effort as phosphocreatine stores deplete.
The aerobic contribution increases progressively as the race continues, and hydrogen ion accumulation causes the characteristic slowing over the final 100 metres.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: Oxygen uptake at the onset of exercise
points.detail: The oxygen deficit at the start of exercise, the attainment of steady state, and the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption during recovery.

questions.q: Explain the oxygen deficit and steady state using a graph of oxygen consumption against time for submaximal exercise.
answer: At the onset of exercise, oxygen demand rises immediately but oxygen supply increases more slowly, creating an oxygen deficit.
The shortfall is met by the anaerobic systems, which supply ATP until oxygen delivery catches up.
Steady state occurs when oxygen supply equals oxygen demand, so the aerobic system meets the full ATP requirement and the plot plateaus.
Steady state can only be reached at submaximal intensities; above the lactate inflection point, demand continues to exceed supply.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: Acute cardiovascular responses
points.detail: Changes in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure, blood flow redistribution and a-vO2 difference during exercise.

questions.q: Describe four acute cardiovascular responses to submaximal exercise and their purpose.
answer: Heart rate increases in proportion to intensity, raising the volume of blood pumped per minute.
Stroke volume increases up to roughly 40 to 60 per cent of maximum intensity, after which it plateaus.
Cardiac output, the product of heart rate and stroke volume, increases substantially to deliver more oxygenated blood to the working muscles.
Blood is redistributed from the organs and gut to the working muscles and skin, and the a-vO2 difference increases as muscles extract more oxygen.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Energy systems and acute responses
points.title: Acute respiratory and muscular responses
points.detail: Changes in respiratory rate, tidal volume, ventilation and gaseous exchange, and in muscle temperature, blood flow and motor unit recruitment.

questions.q: Describe the acute respiratory responses to exercise and their function.
answer: Respiratory rate and tidal volume both increase, raising ventilation, which is the volume of air moved per minute.
Increased ventilation maintains the concentration gradients for oxygen and carbon dioxide at the alveoli.
Gaseous exchange at both the lungs and the muscles increases, supplying more oxygen and removing more carbon dioxide.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Fatigue and recovery
points.title: Fatigue mechanisms
points.detail: Fuel depletion of phosphocreatine and glycogen, metabolic by-product accumulation, thermoregulatory fatigue and neuromuscular fatigue.

questions.q: Identify the likely fatigue mechanism in a marathon runner at 35 kilometres and in a 200 metre sprinter, and justify each.
answer: The marathon runner is most likely experiencing glycogen depletion, since muscle and liver glycogen stores are limited and the aerobic system has been predominant for hours.
Depletion forces greater reliance on fat, which produces ATP more slowly, so pace falls; dehydration and thermoregulatory fatigue also contribute.
The 200 metre sprinter is most likely experiencing accumulation of hydrogen ions from anaerobic glycolysis.
The resulting drop in muscle pH inhibits enzyme activity and calcium binding, reducing the force of contraction.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Fatigue and recovery
points.title: Passive and active recovery
points.detail: The circumstances in which each is appropriate, and the effect of light activity on the removal of metabolic by-products.

questions.q: Explain when passive recovery is preferable to active recovery, and why active recovery suits the removal of metabolic by-products.
answer: Passive recovery is preferable between repeated maximal efforts of short duration, because it allows the fastest restoration of phosphocreatine stores.
Active recovery maintains elevated blood flow to the working muscles after high intensity anaerobic exercise.
Elevated blood flow increases the rate at which hydrogen ions and lactate are transported away and metabolised.
It is therefore preferred after events dominated by anaerobic glycolysis, typically at around 30 to 40 per cent of maximum intensity.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 2 — Fatigue and recovery
points.title: Recovery strategies
points.detail: Rehydration, refuelling and the glycogen window, cool downs, compression, hydrotherapy, massage and sleep, and the evidence for each.

questions.q: Describe three recovery strategies an athlete could use after a tournament match and the mechanism of each.
answer: Rehydration with fluid and electrolytes restores plasma volume and supports thermoregulation and cardiovascular function.
Carbohydrate intake soon after exercise exploits the period of elevated glycogen synthesis to restore muscle glycogen stores.
An active cool down maintains blood flow to assist removal of metabolic by-products and reduce blood pooling.
Adequate sleep supports tissue repair and hormonal recovery, and is among the most strongly supported recovery strategies.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Activity analysis
points.detail: Using movement patterns, skill frequencies, work to rest ratios, heart rate data and time in motion analysis to determine the fitness and energy system requirements of an activity.

questions.q: Explain what an activity analysis involves and how it informs a training program.
answer: An activity analysis collects data on the physiological demands of an activity, including movement patterns, distances covered, skill frequencies and durations.
Work to rest ratios and heart rate data indicate the intensity and the predominant energy system.
This identifies the fitness components most important to performance in that activity.
The training program can then target those specific components and replicate the work to rest ratios of competition, applying the principle of specificity.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Work to rest ratios
points.detail: Calculating work to rest ratios from activity data and using them to identify the predominant energy system and to design interval training.

questions.q: An analysis shows a work to rest ratio of 1 to 5 with efforts of about 6 seconds. Identify the predominant energy system and justify the conclusion.
answer: The ATP-PC system is predominant.
Efforts of around 6 seconds at maximal intensity are supplied primarily by phosphocreatine stores.
A long recovery relative to work, at 1 to 5, allows substantial restoration of phosphocreatine between efforts, so the same system can supply each repeat.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Aerobic power
points.detail: Definition, the role of VO2 max, the factors affecting it, and the tests used to assess it including the multistage fitness test.

questions.q: Define aerobic power and name a valid field test for it, stating one limitation of that test.
answer: Aerobic power is the ability of the body to take in, transport and use oxygen to produce energy aerobically over an extended period.
The multistage fitness test, or beep test, is a valid field test that estimates VO2 max from the level reached.
A limitation is that it only estimates VO2 max rather than measuring it directly, and the result is affected by motivation, running technique and surface.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Anaerobic capacity and muscular power
points.detail: Definitions and tests for anaerobic capacity, muscular power and speed, including the phosphate recovery test, vertical jump and sprint tests.

questions.q: Distinguish between muscular power and muscular strength and name a test for each.
answer: Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single contraction, tested by a one repetition maximum lift or grip dynamometer.
Muscular power is the ability to exert a large force rapidly, combining strength and speed, tested by a vertical jump or standing long jump.
Power is more relevant to explosive sporting actions, since most require force applied quickly rather than maximum force applied slowly.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition
points.detail: Definitions, the tests used, and the relevance of each component to particular activities.

questions.q: Define muscular endurance and explain why it is important to a rower.
answer: Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to sustain repeated contractions over an extended period without fatiguing.
A rower performs a continuous, repeated contraction of the legs, trunk and arms for the duration of the race.
Without muscular endurance, local muscular fatigue would reduce stroke power well before aerobic capacity became limiting.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Agility, balance, coordination and reaction time
points.detail: The skill-related fitness components, their definitions, appropriate tests and their contribution to performance.

questions.q: Define agility and name a test for it, explaining what the test measures.
answer: Agility is the ability to change direction of the whole body rapidly and accurately while maintaining control.
The Illinois agility run is a common test, requiring sprinting, weaving and rapid changes of direction over a set course.
The time taken reflects the athlete's ability to decelerate, change direction and reaccelerate efficiently.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Activity analysis and fitness
points.title: Fitness testing protocols
points.detail: The importance of standardised protocols, validity and reliability, and the pre-test conditions that affect results.

questions.q: Explain why standardised protocols matter in fitness testing and name two pre-test conditions that must be controlled.
answer: Standardised protocols ensure the test measures the same thing in the same way each time, which supports reliability.
Without them, a change in score may reflect a change in testing conditions rather than a change in fitness.
Pre-test conditions to control include time since the last meal and the last training session, and hydration status.
Time of day, footwear, surface and the standardised warm-up should also be kept consistent between pre-test and post-test.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Principle of specificity
points.detail: Matching the training method, muscle groups, movement patterns, energy systems and intensity to the demands of the activity.

questions.q: Explain the principle of specificity and apply it to a 1500 metre runner.
answer: Specificity requires that training match the fitness components, muscle groups, movement patterns and energy systems used in the activity.
A 1500 metre runner relies heavily on aerobic power with a significant anaerobic glycolysis contribution, so training must target both.
Training should therefore be running based rather than cycling based, and should include intervals at race pace as well as continuous aerobic work.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Progressive overload
points.detail: Increasing frequency, intensity, duration or type over time so that the body continues to adapt, and the consequences of progressing too quickly.

questions.q: Explain progressive overload and one risk of applying it too aggressively.
answer: Progressive overload requires that the training stimulus be increased over time, since the body adapts to a given load and further improvement then stops.
Overload can be applied by increasing frequency, intensity or duration, or by changing the type of training.
Progressing too quickly increases the risk of overtraining and injury, because the body is not given sufficient recovery to adapt to the previous load.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Frequency, intensity, duration and training zones
points.detail: Setting the frequency, intensity and duration appropriate to the target fitness component, and calculating heart rate training zones.

questions.q: Explain how to calculate an aerobic training zone using maximum heart rate, and state a typical zone for aerobic power.
answer: Estimate maximum heart rate as 220 minus the athlete's age in years, though a measured maximum is more accurate.
Multiply that maximum by the lower and upper percentages of the target zone to obtain the beats per minute range.
Aerobic training is commonly prescribed at roughly 70 to 85 per cent of maximum heart rate.
Training below the zone provides insufficient stimulus to improve aerobic power, while training above it shifts the emphasis to anaerobic systems.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Diminishing returns, variety, maintenance and detraining
points.detail: The slowing of improvement as an athlete approaches their potential, the need for variety, and the rate at which adaptations are lost when training stops.

questions.q: Explain the principle of diminishing returns and the principle of detraining.
answer: Diminishing returns means that as an athlete becomes fitter, the same training produces progressively smaller improvements.
An untrained person improves rapidly at first, whereas a highly trained athlete needs large increases in load for small gains.
Detraining means adaptations are reversible and are lost when the training stimulus is removed.
Aerobic adaptations begin to decline within about two weeks of inactivity, so a maintenance program is needed during off seasons and injury.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Continuous training
points.detail: Sustained submaximal activity, the intensities and durations used, the fitness components targeted and the adaptations produced.

questions.q: Describe continuous training and state the fitness component it primarily develops.
answer: Continuous training involves sustained aerobic activity with no rest intervals, typically for at least 20 minutes.
It is performed at a submaximal intensity, commonly 70 to 85 per cent of maximum heart rate, so a steady state can be maintained.
It primarily develops aerobic power by improving oxygen delivery and utilisation.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Interval training
points.detail: Short, intermediate and long interval training, the manipulation of work and rest to target a specific energy system, and the relevance of work to rest ratios.

questions.q: Design the work and rest structure of an interval session targeting the ATP-PC system and justify the choices.
answer: Use repeated maximal efforts of about 5 to 10 seconds, such as short sprints, since this is the duration over which the ATP-PC system predominates.
Use a work to rest ratio of about 1 to 5, giving 25 to 50 seconds of passive recovery between efforts.
The long relative recovery allows substantial restoration of phosphocreatine so each repeat can be performed at maximal intensity.
Insufficient recovery would shift the session towards anaerobic glycolysis and reduce the quality of each effort.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Fartlek and circuit training
points.detail: Varied-pace continuous work in fartlek training, and the station-based structure, work to rest design and versatility of circuit training.

questions.q: Explain why fartlek training is particularly suited to team sport athletes.
answer: Fartlek training varies pace continuously between low, moderate and high intensity within a single session.
This replicates the intermittent demands of team sports, where periods of jogging are interspersed with sprints and recovery.
It therefore trains both the aerobic and anaerobic systems in the pattern in which they are used in competition, satisfying specificity.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Resistance training and plyometrics
points.detail: Sets, repetitions and loads for strength, power and endurance outcomes, and the stretch-shorten cycle in plyometric training.

questions.q: State the loading approach for developing muscular strength compared with muscular endurance, and explain how plyometrics develops power.
answer: Muscular strength is developed with heavy loads, typically above 80 per cent of one repetition maximum, for low repetitions of around 1 to 6 and long rests.
Muscular endurance is developed with light loads, typically below 60 per cent, for high repetitions of 15 or more with short rests.
Plyometrics uses a rapid eccentric contraction immediately followed by a powerful concentric contraction, exploiting the stretch-shorten cycle.
The stored elastic energy and stretch reflex increase force production, developing power for jumping and sprinting.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Chronic cardiovascular and respiratory adaptations
points.detail: Cardiac hypertrophy, increased stroke volume and blood volume, reduced resting and submaximal heart rate, capillarisation and increased VO2 max.

questions.q: Explain why an aerobically trained athlete has a lower resting heart rate than an untrained person.
answer: Aerobic training produces hypertrophy of the left ventricle, increasing its internal volume and the force of contraction.
Increased blood volume also improves venous return and ventricular filling.
Together these increase stroke volume, so more blood is ejected with each beat.
Because cardiac output at rest is unchanged, the heart can meet the same demand with fewer beats per minute, producing bradycardia.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Chronic muscular and metabolic adaptations
points.detail: Increased mitochondria, myoglobin, oxidative enzymes, glycogen and phosphocreatine stores, fibre hypertrophy and improved lactate inflection point.

questions.q: Describe three chronic muscular adaptations to aerobic training and their effect on performance.
answer: Increased size and number of mitochondria raise the capacity for aerobic ATP production within the muscle.
Increased myoglobin improves the storage and transport of oxygen within the muscle fibre.
Increased oxidative enzymes and capillarisation improve the rate of oxygen extraction and fuel metabolism.
Together these raise the lactate inflection point, so the athlete can work at a higher intensity before anaerobic glycolysis predominates.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Periodisation
points.detail: Macrocycles, mesocycles and microcycles, the preparatory, competition and transition phases, and tapering before competition.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of periodisation and describe what happens during a taper.
answer: Periodisation divides the training year into cycles so that peak performance coincides with major competition and the risk of overtraining is reduced.
The preparatory phase builds a general base and then sport-specific fitness, the competition phase maintains fitness and sharpens skills, and the transition phase allows recovery.
A taper reduces training volume substantially in the one to three weeks before competition while maintaining intensity.
This allows full recovery, restoration of glycogen and dissipation of accumulated fatigue without losing the adaptations already gained.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Psychological strategies
points.detail: Goal setting, mental imagery, self-talk, confidence, arousal regulation and concentration, and their application in training and competition.

questions.q: Explain how goal setting and mental imagery can improve performance.
answer: Goal setting directs attention and effort, and specific measurable goals allow progress to be monitored and sustained motivation.
A combination of outcome, performance and process goals is most effective, since process goals remain within the athlete's control.
Mental imagery rehearses the skill or the competitive situation without physical execution, reinforcing the motor pattern.
It also allows the athlete to prepare emotionally for pressure situations, which supports arousal regulation and confidence.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Training programs and adaptations
points.title: Nutrition and hydration strategies
points.detail: Carbohydrate loading, pre-event, during-event and post-event nutrition, hydration and the use of legal aids.

questions.q: Explain carbohydrate loading and describe an appropriate during-event nutrition strategy for a road cyclist.
answer: Carbohydrate loading increases carbohydrate intake in the days before a prolonged endurance event while training volume is tapered.
This maximises muscle and liver glycogen stores, delaying the onset of glycogen depletion during the event.
During the event the cyclist should consume easily digestible carbohydrate, such as gels or sports drink, at regular intervals.
Fluid with electrolytes should be consumed regularly rather than only when thirsty, to limit the fall in plasma volume and support thermoregulation.

points.area: Data collection and exam technique
points.title: Collecting and interpreting data
points.detail: Using heart rate monitors, GPS, video and lactate data, and interpreting graphs of heart rate, oxygen consumption and blood lactate.

questions.q: Explain how to interpret a graph of blood lactate against exercise intensity and identify the lactate inflection point.
answer: Blood lactate remains relatively low and stable at low intensities, because it is produced and removed at similar rates.
The lactate inflection point is where the curve rises sharply, indicating production has begun to exceed removal.
It is usually expressed as a percentage of VO2 max, and a trained athlete's inflection point occurs at a higher percentage.
A higher inflection point indicates the athlete can sustain a greater intensity before fatiguing by-products accumulate.

points.area: Data collection and exam technique
points.title: Justifying with data
points.detail: Referring to specific values, units and trends from stimulus material rather than making general statements, and linking the data to physiological reasoning.

questions.q: Explain what a question asking you to 'justify your answer using the data' requires.
answer: Quote specific values from the stimulus with their units, such as a heart rate in beats per minute or a distance in metres.
State the trend or comparison the values demonstrate, for example that one athlete's value is higher at the same intensity.
Link the data to the physiological explanation, since the data alone without reasoning does not answer the question.

points.area: Data collection and exam technique
points.title: Command terms and mark allocation
points.detail: Matching the depth of response to the command term and mark value, and answering every part of a multi-part question.

questions.q: Explain how the command terms 'identify', 'explain' and 'evaluate' differ in the response they require.
answer: Identify requires only naming the correct item, such as a fitness component or energy system, with no elaboration.
Explain requires reasons and the physiological mechanism, showing how or why the outcome occurs.
Evaluate requires weighing strengths against limitations and reaching a supported judgement.
The mark allocation indicates how many distinct points are required, so a four-mark explain question needs about four linked points.
